summary:
Cundinamarca is a department of Colombia and stands directly under the national legal framework. The source inventory carries no finding on law, enforcement practice or recorded incidents specific to this department, so a visitor's expectations rest on how the national rules apply and on the national enforcement record.

Legal gender recognition runs through an administrative channel rather than a court. Since 1993 a person may change the gender marker on a Colombian birth certificate, with current options of F, M, NB (no binario) and T (transgénero); the process is notarial and requires no surgery and no court ruling, and the sources state that it applies equally in Cundinamarca. Decree 0732 of 2026, signed by outgoing justice minister Jorge Iván Cuervo on 9 July 2026, obliges public notaries to complete the request within five business days, makes the first request and any simultaneous name change free of charge, and shields the change history from public disclosure.

The non-binary marker exists by court order. The Constitutional Court's 4 February 2022 ruling ordered the government to offer the NB option to everyone and to ask Congress to amend the relevant laws, and since August 2023 passports issued within Colombia offer three gender options: male, female and X.

Documentary practice has not always matched the rules. A 2016 report, Cartografía de derechos trans in Colombia, by OutRight Action International, El Aquelarre Trans and PAIIS, documented notaries refusing to process name changes and recommended ending the psychiatric pathologisation of transgender identity.

Violence risk is documented nationally rather than for this department. In 2023, 41 trans women were killed in Colombia, with a further eight between February and April 2024. Armed groups in Caquetá gave trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed and circulated 'social cleansing' flyers against trans women. Reporting of 6 August 2025 covers the wave of attacks against LGBTQ+ people following the killing of Sara Millerey. The inventory contains no Cundinamarca-specific incident data.
tangentialFactors:
An advocate quoted in the 30 July 2024 Guardian investigation states that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording such killings as ordinary cases. That practice shapes how a visitor should read official crime statistics anywhere in Colombia, including Cundinamarca: an absence of transfemicide findings is not evidence that none occurred.

The national armed-group baseline that Cundinamarca is assessed against is one of displacement as well as killing, with trans women in affected departments pushed out of towns under threat and, in some areas, left with few livelihood options beyond sex work.

Colombia's documented gap between institutional reform and lived experience has been noted internationally: the legal instruments covering gender markers, documents and premises access are among the most developed in the region, while the recorded killing rate of trans women has continued to rise.
localsOnly:
Residents of Cundinamarca use the same notarial route as the rest of the country. Decree 0732 of 2026 sets a five-business-day deadline on public notaries for completing a gender-marker request, removes the fee for the first request and for a simultaneous name change, and prevents the change history from being disclosed publicly.

Residents holding Colombian passports have had three gender options (male, female, X) on documents issued within the country since August 2023, and the non-binary marker on other documents rests on the Constitutional Court's 4 February 2022 order.

Local notaries in this department were among the offices identified in the 2016 Cartografía de derechos trans en Colombia report as refusing to process name changes; the report's recommendation to end psychiatric pathologisation of transgender identity remains on the record.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports the text of any Cundinamarca departmental ordinance, local police directive or departmental ombudsman practice bearing on trans visitors, and none is asserted here.

Recorded killings, threat incidents and hate-crime counts specific to Cundinamarca are unresolved: the inventory supplies national figures only, and no department-level breakdown was available.

Whether notaries across Cundinamarca now meet the five-business-day standard set by Decree 0732 of 2026, and whether any office has continued the refusals documented in 2016, is not sourced.

The practical availability of shelters, complaint channels and protection orders for trans visitors within this department is not sourced.
